outcomes.text: Choose the most suitable data type category for a given specification.
A data type specifies values and operations, and is classified as primitive or reference.
Primitive types in this course define numeric and Boolean values and the operations available for them.
Reference types define objects rather than primitive values.
Write declarations for variables that store numbers and Boolean values.
The course uses int for integers, double for real numbers, and boolean for true-or-false values.
A variable is a named, typed storage location whose held value can change during execution.

topics.title: 1.1 Introduction to Algorithms, Programming, and Compilers

outcomes.text: Represent everyday patterns and algorithms using written descriptions or diagrams.
Understand that algorithms are step-by-step procedures represented with words or diagrams.
Understand sequencing as completing process steps one at a time in a defined order.
Explain how source code is compiled and then executed.
Understand that IDEs help programmers write, compile, and run code.
Understand that compilers detect certain errors that must be corrected before execution.
Identify different kinds of programming errors.
Recognize syntax errors as violations of programming-language rules detected by the compiler.
Recognize logic errors as incorrect behavior found by testing program results against expectations.
Recognize run-time errors as mistakes occurring during execution that may terminate a program abnormally.
Recognize exceptions as run-time errors that interrupt normal program execution.
Write output code and determine what appears on the display.
Distinguish print, which stays on the line, from println, which advances to the next line.
Use string literals and determine their resulting values.
Understand a literal as code representing a fixed value.
Recognize a string literal as characters enclosed in double quotation marks.
Use Java escape sequences for quotation marks, backslashes, and newlines.
Write arithmetic expressions and determine their results.
Understand arithmetic expressions as numeric values, variables, and operators producing int or double results.
Apply arithmetic operators and determine whether operations produce int or double results.
Distinguish integer division, which discards the fractional part, from division involving doubles.
Use the remainder operator to find what remains after division.
Evaluate compound expressions using precedence, parentheses, and left-to-right evaluation for equal precedence.
Recognize that integer division by zero causes an ArithmeticException.
Write assignments and determine the resulting stored variable values.
Assign compatible values before variables are used; references may hold objects or null.
Use = to place the right-hand expression’s value into the left-hand variable.
Understand that evaluating an expression produces one value with a resulting type.
Write code that reads input.
Understand that Scanner can obtain text typed at the keyboard.
Cast primitive values in arithmetic expressions and determine the resulting value.
Use int and double casts to convert between those primitive types.
Understand that casting double to int removes digits after the decimal point.
Recognize automatic widening of int values to double values.
Round doubles to nearby integers using appropriate expressions for nonnegative and negative values.
Describe when integer expressions exceed the permitted range.
Use Integer.MAX_VALUE and Integer.MIN_VALUE to identify int boundaries.
Understand that int values occupy finite memory and range between the two Integer constants.
Recognize integer overflow when a calculation exceeds the int range.
Describe conditions that reduce expression accuracy.
Explain round-off error when a double requires more precision than available storage.
Write compound assignments and determine the resulting stored value.
Use compound operators to perform arithmetic and assign the result back to the same variable.
Use post-increment and post-decrement to add or subtract one from numeric variables.
Identify library-class attributes and behaviors using API documentation.
Understand libraries as class collections and APIs as instructions for using their classes.
Distinguish class attributes, stored in variables, from behaviors, defined by methods.
Explain how comments document code and support its use.
Understand Java block, single-line, and Javadoc comments and that comments are not executed.
Define a precondition as a requirement that must hold immediately before a method runs.
Define a postcondition as a condition guaranteed after a method finishes.
Identify which method to call using its documentation and signature.
Understand methods as named code blocks that run when called and support procedural abstraction.
Define parameters and method signatures using method names and ordered parameter types.
Describe how to call methods.
Recognize that void methods return no value and cannot be used within expressions.
Use a non-void method’s returned value in a variable or expression of the appropriate type.
Pass compatible arguments in the required number and order; understand call-by-value parameter copying.
Recognize overloaded methods as methods sharing a name but having different signatures.
Explain how a method call temporarily redirects control before returning to the following statement.
Write calls to class methods and determine their results.
Recognize class methods as static methods associated with the class rather than its instances.
Call class methods using the class name and dot operator, with the class name optional inside that class.
Write expressions using built-in mathematical library calls and determine their results.
Know that Math belongs to java.lang, whose classes are automatically available.
Use Math.abs, Math.pow, Math.sqrt, and Math.random with their specified parameter and return behaviors.
Transform Math.random results with arithmetic and casting to generate values in specified inclusive or exclusive ranges.
Explain the relationship between classes and objects.
Distinguish an object as a class instance with attributes and a class as its blueprint.
Describe superclass-subclass inheritance, including shared attributes and behaviors.
Recognize that every Java class ultimately extends the Object class.
Declare variables that store references to objects.
Understand that a reference variable stores an object reference, conceptually a memory address.
Identify the constructor being called from its signature.
Recognize constructors as class members named after the class and used to create objects.
Identify constructor signatures by class name and ordered parameter types.
Recognize overloaded constructors as constructors with the same name but different signatures.
Declare correctly typed variables for object references.
Understand that a reference variable holds an object reference or null.
Create objects by calling constructors.
Create objects with new followed by a constructor call.
Use constructor parameters to establish initial object attribute values.
Pass constructor arguments matching the required number, order, and types; understand call-by-value copying.
Explain how constructor calls interrupt sequential execution and then return control afterward.
Write calls to instance methods and determine their results.
Call instance methods on objects using the object name and dot operator.
Recognize that calling an instance method through null causes a NullPointerException.
Create and combine strings and determine the resulting values.
Create String objects with literals or the String constructor to represent character sequences.
Recognize String as a java.lang class available without an import.
Understand that String objects are immutable and their methods do not alter existing content.
Concatenate strings with + or +=; primitive values are implicitly converted to strings.
Understand object concatenation invokes toString, which produces a textual representation of the object.
Call String methods and determine their results.
Use valid String indices from zero through length minus one; invalid indices cause an exception.
Use length, substring, indexOf, equals, and compareTo according to their specified behaviors.
Create the single-character string at an index with substring(index, index + 1).
Represent everyday algorithms involving selection and repetition using written language or diagrams.
Algorithms are built from sequencing, selection, and repetition.
Algorithms may use decision-making for selection and looping for repetition.
Selection chooses the execution path according to a true-or-false decision.
Repetition repeatedly performs a process until the desired result is achieved.
The arrangement of sequencing, selection, and repetition affects an algorithm’s result.
Write Boolean expressions with relational operators and determine their results.
The operators == and != compare primitive values or object references, depending on the operand types.
The operators <, >, <=, and >= compare numeric values.
Relational expressions produce Boolean values.
Write selection statements and determine the results of branching processes.
Selection statements alter the sequential flow of program execution.
An if statement executes different code depending on a Boolean expression.
A one-way if executes its body only when its condition is true.
An if-else chooses one of two code segments according to whether its condition is true or false.
Write nested selection statements and determine the results of nested branching processes.
Nested selection places if, if-else, or if-else-if statements inside other selection statements.
An inner condition is evaluated only when the surrounding outer condition is true.
An if-else-if chain selects at most one segment based on the first true condition, or else executes the trailing else.
Write compound Boolean expressions and determine their results.
Use !, &&, and || with Boolean expressions; their precedence is !, then &&, then ||.
Short-circuit evaluation skips the second operand when the first operand determines an && or || result.
Compare Boolean expressions that are equivalent.
Equivalent Boolean expressions have identical values in every case; truth tables can demonstrate this.
Apply De Morgan’s law to produce equivalent forms of negated conjunctions and disjunctions.
Compare object references with Boolean expressions and determine the results.
Different variables can reference the same object, and == or != can compare those references.
Compare an object reference with null using == or != to test whether it references an object.
A class’s equals method can define object equivalence using attributes of the objects.
Recognize when iteration is needed to achieve a desired result.
Iteration repeats code zero or more times while its controlling Boolean expression remains true.
An infinite loop results when its controlling Boolean expression always remains true.
An iterative body does not run when its initial Boolean condition is false.
An off-by-one error makes a loop execute one time too many or too few.
Write while loops for iterative processes and determine their results.
A while loop tests its condition before each iteration, including the first, and stops when the condition becomes false.
Write for loops for iterative processes and determine their results.
A for-loop header contains initialization, a Boolean condition, and an update.
A for loop initializes once, tests its condition before iterations, and updates after each complete body execution.
A for loop can be converted to an equivalent while loop, and vice versa.
Write standard and original algorithms without data structures and determine their results.
Standard algorithms test divisibility, extract digits, count criteria, find extrema, and calculate sums or averages.
Write and evaluate standard or original algorithms that process strings.
Standard string algorithms test substring properties, count qualifying substrings, and reverse characters.
Write nested iterative processes and determine their results.
In nested loops, the inner loop completes all iterations before the outer loop proceeds.
Calculate statement execution counts and informally compare iterative run times.
A statement execution count records how many times a statement runs, often found by tracing loops.
Represent program designs with natural language or diagrams showing classes, attributes, and behaviors.
Design a class’s attributes and behaviors before implementation using language or diagrams.
Understand abstraction as reducing complexity by emphasizing relevant ideas and hiding unnecessary details.
Understand data abstraction as separating a data type’s abstract properties from its concrete representation.
Distinguish attributes, instance variables unique to objects, and class variables shared by all instances.
Use procedural abstraction and method decomposition to break behaviors into reusable, smaller operations.
Use parameters to generalize procedures for reuse with different input values.
Change a method’s implementation without affecting users when its signature and behavior remain unchanged.
Explain social and ethical implications of computing systems.
Recognize that programs can produce beneficial or harmful effects on society, the economy, and culture.
Understand system reliability as performing expected tasks under stated conditions, and maximize it through varied testing.
Recognize legal and intellectual-property requirements when reusing code that is not openly licensed.
Write classes, data, constructors, and methods with appropriate visibility and access restrictions.
Declare course classes as public using the class keyword.
Declare course constructors as public.
Use encapsulation to hide implementation details, applying public and private access appropriately.
Usually declare instance variables private to preserve encapsulation.
Distinguish public methods accessible internally and externally from private methods accessible only internally.
Understand that each object owns its own copy of instance variables.
Write constructors that initialize instance variables representing an object’s attributes.
Understand object state as the current values of its instance variables.
Use constructors to allocate objects and establish initial instance-variable values, optionally from parameters.
Copy mutable constructor arguments when initializing instance variables to prevent unintended changes to the original object.
Understand that Java supplies a no-parameter default constructor when none is written.
Know default values: 0 for int, 0.0 for double, false for boolean, and null for references.
Write methods using primitive values and determine their results when called.
Use parameter values within methods to perform their intended tasks.
Recognize that void methods do not return values and include void in their headers.
Recognize that non-void methods return one value and specify its type in the header.
Return an expression compatible with a non-void method’s declared return type.
Use return to exit a method or constructor; later statements and enclosing control flow may not execute.
Understand accessor methods as non-void methods that provide copies of variable values.
Understand mutator methods as methods that change instance or class variable values, often returning void.
Understand that primitive arguments initialize parameters with copies, so parameter changes do not affect arguments.

topics.title: 3.6 Methods: Passing and Returning References of Objects

outcomes.text: Write methods using object references and determine their results when called.
Understand that object-reference parameters alias the same object and can change mutable object state.
Understand that returning an object expression returns its reference, not a newly copied object.
Access private members of a referenced parameter only when its type matches the enclosing class.
Write class methods that define class-level behaviors.
Understand that class methods need an instance parameter to access instance variables or methods.
Understand that class methods can access class variables and call other class methods.
Write declarations for class variables shared by a class’s objects.
Declare shared class variables with static; all instances use one copy.
Access public class variables externally through the class name and dot operator.
Understand that final variables cannot be assigned new values.
Explain where variables may be used within a program.
Understand that local variables and parameters are usable only within their declaring method, constructor, or block.
When names conflict, a local variable or parameter takes precedence over an instance variable.
Write self-referencing expressions and determine their results.
Within an instance method or constructor, this refers to the object whose code is executing.
Use this to pass the current object as an argument in a method call.
Recognize that class methods do not have access to a this reference.

topics.title: 4.1 Ethical and Social Issues Around Data Collection

outcomes.text: Explain privacy risks when personal data is collected and stored on computer systems.
Personal privacy can be endangered by computer use, so programs should protect users’ personal information.
Explain why data quality and possible problems must be considered when using a data set.
Algorithmic bias consists of systematic, repeated programming errors that produce unfair outcomes for a particular user group.
Consider how data-collection methods and their possible biases affect extrapolations and conclusions.
Recognize that incomplete or inaccurate data can make programs incorrect or inefficient.
Select a suitable data set for solving a problem or answering a particular question.
A data set may fit one question or topic but be unsuitable for answering or extrapolating to another.
Represent everyday data-set patterns and algorithms using written descriptions or diagrams.
A data set is a collection of specific information or data.
Data sets can be analyzed and manipulated by processing individual values to solve problems or answer questions.
Charts and tables can depict data and help plan algorithms for manipulating it.
Write code representing related collections with one-dimensional array objects.
An array holds multiple values of one type, either primitive values or object references.
An array’s fixed length is set at creation and retrieved through its length attribute.
New arrays initialize elements with type-specific defaults: 0, 0.0, false, or null.
Initializer lists can create and initialize arrays.
Use square-bracket indices to access or change one-dimensional array elements.
Valid array indices range from zero through length minus one; other indices cause ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Write traversals of one-dimensional arrays and determine their results.
Array traversal uses repetition to access all elements or an ordered sequence of elements.
Indexed for and while loops access array elements through their indices.
An enhanced for loop assigns each element’s copy to a loop variable without using an index.
Changing an enhanced for loop variable does not alter the corresponding array element.
For object-reference arrays, methods called through the enhanced loop variable can modify objects, not stored references.
Rewrite an enhanced for traversal as an indexed for loop or while loop.
Develop and evaluate standard or original array algorithms for a specified context.
Array-traversal algorithms can find extrema, calculate sums or averages, test properties, count matches, inspect pairs, detect duplicates, shift, rotate, or reverse elements.
Write code that reads data from a text file.
A file persistently stores data that programs can retrieve during execution.
Connect a file to a program with the File and Scanner classes.
Create a File object with the file pathname to open that file for reading.
Handle failure to open a file, such as by declaring IOException; an invalid filename terminates the program.
Import File and IOException from the java.io package before using them.
Use Scanner’s file constructor and methods to read typed values, lines, tokens, test availability, and close the scanner.
Mixing nextLine with other Scanner methods may require adjustments for their different whitespace handling.
Use String.split to produce substrings separated around matches of a specified delimiter expression.
Use hasNext as a while-loop condition to detect whether a file has more elements.
Close the Scanner when finished reading the file.
Use Integer and Double wrapper objects and determine the results of using them.
Integer and Double objects are immutable classes in java.lang.
Autoboxing automatically converts primitives to corresponding wrapper objects when required by assignments or method parameters.
Unboxing automatically converts wrapper objects to corresponding primitives for assignments or method parameters.
Integer.parseInt converts a String argument into an int.
Double.parseDouble converts a String argument into a double.
Write code using ArrayList collections and predict the results of calling their methods.
Understand that ArrayList objects can change size and store references to objects.
Know that ArrayList() creates an empty list.
Use generic ArrayList<E> types to specify element, parameter, and return types and catch errors during compilation.
Import ArrayList from the java.util package before using it.
Know how ArrayList size, add, get, set, and remove methods behave and what they return.
Use ArrayList indices from zero through one less than the list size.
Write ArrayList traversals and determine their results.
Traverse an ArrayList by iterating or recursively accessing all or an ordered sequence of elements.
Use techniques that prevent skipped elements when deleting during an ArrayList traversal.
Recognize that an invalid ArrayList index causes an IndexOutOfBoundsException.
Avoid adding or removing elements during enhanced-for traversal because changing size can cause ConcurrentModificationException.
Develop and evaluate standard or original algorithms involving ArrayList traversals.
Use ArrayList traversals for extrema, aggregates, property tests, counting, pairs, duplicates, shifts, reversals, insertion, and deletion.
Traverse multiple String, array, or ArrayList objects simultaneously when an algorithm requires it.
Write code representing related data with two-dimensional array objects.
Create and initialize 2D arrays with nested initializer lists representing rows.
Understand 2D arrays as arrays of arrays with fixed size that can store primitives or object references.
Know that newly created 2D array elements receive type-specific default values.
Use row and column indices to access or modify 2D array elements.
Access a complete row of a 2D array using the array name and row index.
Use length to determine valid row and column indices and recognize invalid indices as exceptions.
Write 2D array traversals and determine their results.
Use nested iteration to traverse 2D arrays in row-major, column-major, or other specified orders.
Use correctly typed variables in nested enhanced-for loops and understand that changing loop variables does not modify array elements.
Develop and evaluate standard or original algorithms involving 2D array traversals.
Use 2D traversals for extrema, aggregates, property tests, counting, pairs, duplicates, shifts, rotations, and reversals.
Write linear searches for information in collections and determine their results.
Understand linear searches that check array or ArrayList elements sequentially from either end.
Search a 2D array linearly by processing each row in turn.
Determine the result of each step when sorting collection elements.
Recognize selection sort and insertion sort as iterative algorithms for arrays and ArrayLists.
Understand selection sort selecting an extreme unsorted element and swapping it into its final position.
Understand insertion sort shifting sorted elements to insert an unsorted element into its appropriate position.
Determine the results of calling recursive methods.
Understand that recursive methods call themselves, include a stopping base case, and contain a recursive call.
Understand that each recursive call has separate local variables and parameters tracking process progress.
Recognize that recursive and iterative approaches can implement equivalent solutions.
Determine the result of executing recursive algorithms that use strings or collections.
Recursion can traverse String objects, arrays, and ArrayList objects.
Determine the result of each iteration of a binary search algorithm used on a collection.
Binary search requires sorted data, examines the middle, and recursively eliminates half the remaining collection.
Binary search is generally more efficient than linear search.
Binary search may be implemented iteratively or recursively.
Determine the result of each iteration of merge sort when sorting a collection.
Merge sort recursively sorts elements in an array or ArrayList.
Merge sort repeatedly splits arrays into single-element subarrays, then merges them into sorted order.
